claim: Human behaviour requires flexible arbitration between actions we do out of habit and actions that are directed towards a specific goal.
source: Human behaviour requires flexible arbitration between actions we do out of habit and actions that are directed towards a specific goal.
evidence: This is a general statement about human behavior that draws from established understanding in cognitive science and psychology.

claim: Drugs that target opioid and dopamine receptors are notorious for inducing maladaptive habitual drug consumption.
source: Drugs that target opioid and dopamine receptors are notorious for inducing maladaptive habitual drug consumption
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about addiction and drug effects.

claim: The administration of the dopamine D2/3 receptor antagonist amisulpride led to an increase in goal-directed or 'model-based' relative to habitual or 'model-free' behaviour.
source: the administration of the dopamine D2/3 receptor antagonist amisulpride led to an increase in goal-directed or 'model-based' relative to habitual or 'model-free' behaviour
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental study with 112 participants using the two-step task and computational modeling.

claim: The non-selective opioid receptor antagonist naltrexone had no appreciable effect on model-based/model-free behaviour.
source: the non-selective opioid receptor antagonist naltrexone had no appreciable effect
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental study comparing naltrexone to placebo.

claim: The effect of amisulpride on model-based/model-free behaviour did not scale with drug serum levels in the blood.
source: The effect of amisulpride on model-based/model-free behaviour did not scale with drug serum levels in the blood.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of blood serum levels and computational modeling parameters.

claim: Participants with higher amisulpride serum levels showed higher explorative behaviour.
source: participants with higher amisulpride serum levels showed higher explorative behaviour
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the inverse temperature parameter in relation to serum levels.

claim: Even small doses of amisulpride promote flexible application of cognitive control.
source: even small doses of amisulpride promote flexible application of cognitive control
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that amisulpride effects did not scale with serum levels.

claim: Several theories of decision making postulate the existence of two distinct systems that drive our behaviour: a habitual system, which is automatic, reflexive and fast; and a goal-directed system, which is deliberative, reflective and effortful.
source: Several theories of decision making postulate the existence of two distinct systems that drive our behaviour: a habitual system, which is automatic, reflexive and fast; and a goal-directed system, which is deliberative, reflective and effortful (Dickinson, 1985; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: This dichotomy of systems has a computational analogue in 'model-free' and 'model-based' decision-making models.
source: This dichotomy of systems has a computational analogue in 'model-free' and 'model-based' decision-making models (Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Daw et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claim: A model-free agent simply selects actions that have led to rewarding outcomes in the past.
source: A model-free agent simply selects actions that have led to rewarding outcomes in the past.
evidence: This is a definition based on established computational modeling frameworks.

claim: Model-free strategy is fast, computationally cheap, but can be inaccurate.
source: This strategy is fast, computationally cheap, but can be inaccurate.
evidence: This characterization is based on established understanding of model-free reinforcement learning.

claim: A model-based agent uses an internal model of the environment to flexibly plan behavioural responses.
source: A model-based agent uses an internal model of the environment to flexibly plan behavioural responses.
evidence: This is a definition based on established computational modeling frameworks.

claim: Model-based behaviour leads to more goal-oriented behaviour but is slower and relies on effortful cognitive control.
source: This leads to more goal-oriented behaviour but is slower and relies on effortful cognitive control.
evidence: This characterization is based on established understanding of model-based reinforcement learning.

claim: Model-based control is increased when there is more to gain.
source: Studies investigating how individuals allocate control between the two systems have shown that model-based control is increased when there is more to gain (Patzelt et al., 2019; Kool et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior empirical studies.

claim: Model-based control is decreased when cognitive resources are scarce.
source: decreased when cognitive resources are scarce (Otto et al., 2013b; Otto et al., 2013a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior empirical studies.

claim: Everyday behaviour can be thought of as constant weighing of costs and benefits of applying model-based over model-free decision-making strategies.
source: Everyday behaviour can therefore be thought of as constant weighing of costs and benefits of applying model-based over model-free decision-making strategies (Kool et al., 2017; Daw et al., 2011; Kool and Botvinick, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Failure to exert cognitive control over habitual urges in order to avoid negative outcomes has been suggested to be a hallmark of substance addiction.
source: Failure to exert cognitive control over habitual urges in order to avoid negative outcomes has been suggested to be a hallmark of substance addiction (Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Everitt et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work on addiction.

claim: Decreased model-based control is linked to stimulant use disorder.
source: studies show that decreased model-based control is linked to stimulant use disorder (Voon et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior empirical study.

claim: Decreased model-based control seems to constitute a transdiagnostic dimensional trait related to compulsive behaviour across clinical and non-clinical populations.
source: seems to constitute a transdiagnostic dimensional trait related to compulsive behaviour across clinical (Voon et al., 2015; Voon et al., 2017) and non-clinical populations (Gillan et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior empirical studies.

claim: Opiates, psychostimulants, and most other drugs of abuse increase the release of dopamine along the mesolimbic pathway.
source: Opiates, psychostimulants, and most other drugs of abuse increase the release of dopamine along the mesolimbic pathway (Koob and Bloom, 1988; Di Chiara, 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neurobiological research.

claim: The mesolimbic pathway plays a central role in reinforcement learning.
source: a circuit that plays a central role in reinforcement learning (Schultz et al., 1997)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior neurobiological research.

claim: The reinforcing properties of addictive drugs depend on their ability to activate the µ opioid receptors.
source: the reinforcing properties of addictive drugs also depend on their ability to activate the µ opioid receptors (Le Merrer et al., 2009; Benjamin et al., 1993; Becker et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neurobiological research.

claim: Activating receptors of both dopamine and opioid systems across the striatum increases cue-triggered wanting of rewards in rodents.
source: Studies in rodents show that activating receptors of both systems across the striatum increases cue-triggered wanting of rewards (Peciña and Berridge, 2013; Soares-Cunha et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Inhibition of both D1-type and D2-type dopamine receptors as well as opioid receptors reduces motivation to obtain or consume rewards.
source: Conversely, inhibition of both D1-type and D2-type dopamine receptors (referred to as D1 and D2 from here on) as well as opioid receptors reduces motivation to obtain or consume rewards (Soares-Cunha et al., 2016; Laurent et al., 2012; Peciña, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Systemic administration of opioid and D2 dopamine receptor antagonists causes a comparable reduction of cue responsivity and reward impulsivity in humans.
source: Recent work in humans provides some evidence in this direction, whereby systemic administration of opioid and D2 dopamine receptor antagonists causes a comparable reduction of cue responsivity and reward impulsivity (Weber et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior human study.

claim: Opioid and D2 dopamine receptor antagonists decrease the effort to obtain immediate primary rewards in humans.
source: decreases the effort to obtain immediate primary rewards (Korb et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior human study.

claim: Opioid receptor antagonists did not have an effect on tasks in which exertion of cognitive control plays a key role, such as working memory, sustained attention, or mathematical problem-solving.
source: Across a wide range of studies using various dosing schemes, opioid receptor antagonists did not have an effect on tasks in which exertion of cognitive control plays a key role, such as working memory (File and Silverstone, 1981; Volavka et al., 1979; Martín del Campo et al., 1992), sustained attention (Zacny et al., 1994), or mathematical problem-solving (Martín del Campo et al., 1992) (see van Steenbergen et al., 2019 for a review).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple prior studies and a review.

claim: Dopaminergic circuits are central in a variety of higher cognitive functions and goal-directed behaviour.
source: Dopaminergic circuits, on the other hand, are central in a variety of higher cognitive functions and goal-directed behaviour (Brozoski et al., 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: D1 dopamine receptors in the prefrontal cortex enable the maintenance of goal-relevant information and working memory.
source: In particular, D1 dopamine receptors in the prefrontal cortex enable the maintenance of goal-relevant information and working memory (van Schouwenburg et al., 2010; Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Williams and Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Goldman-Rakic, 1997)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neurobiological research.

claim: D2 dopamine receptor activity disrupts prefrontal representations.
source: while the D2 dopamine receptor activity disrupts prefrontal representations (Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Decreased working memory performance was observed after blocking prefrontal D1, but not prefrontal D2 receptors.
source: In support of this, decreased working memory performance was observed after blocking prefrontal D1, but not prefrontal D2 receptors (Sawaguchi and Goldman-Rakic, 1991; Arnsten, 2011; Seamans and Yang, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Systemic administration of D2 antagonism increased the ability to maintain and manipulate working memory representations in humans.
source: In humans, systemic administration of D2 antagonism increased the ability to maintain and manipulate working memory representations (Dodds et al., 2009; Frank and O'Reilly, 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claim: D2 antagonism increased the value of applying cognitive effort in humans.
source: increased the value of applying cognitive effort (Westbrook et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior human study.

claim: The study tested 112 participants with a deterministic version of the two-step task.
source: We tested 112 participants with a deterministic version of the two-step task (Daw et al., 2005; Kool et al., 2016), at baseline and after administering amisulpride (N=38, 400 mg), naltrexone (N=39, 50 mg), or placebo (N=35) in a randomized, double-blind, between-subject design (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: The study used a randomized, double-blind, between-subject design.
source: in a randomized, double-blind, between-subject design (Figure 1)
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Participants often failed to consider the mapping from spaceship to planets when making choices in trials where the first stage state differed from the previous trial.
source: This indicates that participants often failed to consider the mapping from spaceship to planets when making choices in trials where the first stage state differed from the previous trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: There was no difference in mood changes following amisulpride administration from drug intake and 3 hr in either serum group.
source: We also found no difference in mood changes following amisulpride administration from drug intake and 3 hr in either serum group (Supplementary file 1cd and e)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the mood questionnaire analysis.

claim: Naltrexone flattened both positive and negative affect.
source: but found that naltrexone flattened both positive (b=–0.411, 95% CI [–0.855, 0.029], P(b>0)=0.035) and negative affect (b=–0.524, 95% CI [-1.001,–0.061], P(b>0)=0.013)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the mood questionnaire analysis.

claim: The findings provide initial evidence for a divergent involvement of the dopamine and opioid neurotransmitter systems in the shift between habitual and goal-directed behaviour.
source: Our findings provide initial evidence for a divergent involvement of the dopamine and opioid neurotransmitter systems in the shift between habitual and goal-directed behaviour.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings of the study.

claim: The lack of effects of naltrexone on the model-based/model-free trade-off provides some support for the notion that simply disrupting neurobiological systems that subserve habitual behaviour might not be enough to increase goal-directed behaviour in this task.
source: The lack of effects of naltrexone on the model-based/model-free trade-off also provides some support for the notion that simply disrupting neurobiological systems that subserve habitual behaviour might not be enough to increase goal-directed behaviour in this task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the naltrexone findings.

claim: An increase in the model-based/model-free weight following amisulpride administration advocates for dopamine playing a decisive role in flexibly applying cognitive control to facilitate model-based behaviour.
source: An increase in the model-based/model-free weight following amisulpride administration advocates for dopamine playing a decisive role in flexibly applying cognitive control to facilitate model-based behaviour
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amisulpride findings.

claim: The findings highlight the specific functional contribution of the D2 receptor subtype.
source: highlights the specific functional contribution of the D2 receptor subtype
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amisulpride findings.

claim: Elevated dopamine levels, either at baseline or following pharmacological treatments such as L-dopa, are related to increased model-based behaviour in some studies.
source: Elevated dopamine levels, either at baseline or following pharmacological treatments such as L-dopa, are related to increased model-based behaviour in some studies (Wunderlich et al., 2012; Deserno et al., 2015; Sharp et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Elevated dopamine levels show no correlation or even opposite effects on model-based behaviour in other studies.
source: but show no correlation or even opposite effects in others (Kroemer et al., 2019; Voon et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: According to the dual-state theory of prefrontal dopamine function, a state dominated by D1 receptor activity is characterized by a high-energy barrier and supports stabilization of prefrontal representations.
source: According to the dual-state theory of prefrontal dopamine function (Durstewitz and Seamans, 2008), a state dominated by D1 receptor activity is characterized by a high-energy barrier and supports stabilization of prefrontal representations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: According to the dual-state theory, a D2 receptor dominated state has a low-energy barrier and facilitates flexible switching between representational states.
source: Conversely, a D2 receptor dominated state has a low-energy barrier and facilitates flexible switching between representational states.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: D2 antagonists impair behaviour in tasks that require constant attentional set shifting.
source: In line with this, D2 antagonists impair behaviour in tasks that require constant attentional set shifting (Mehta et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: D2 antagonists might improve performance in tasks where prefrontal goal representations are required.
source: but might improve performance in tasks where prefrontal goal representations are required (Kahnt et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: D2 antagonism does not improve working memory capacity, or memory retrieval.
source: but does not improve working memory capacity, or memory retrieval (Dodds et al., 2009; Naef et al., 2017; Mehta et al., 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Phasic dopaminergic bursts subserve prediction error propagation and action initiation mainly, but not exclusively, through D1 dopamine receptors.
source: In the striatum, phasic dopaminergic bursts subserve prediction error propagation and action initiation (Frank et al., 2004) mainly, but not exclusively, through D1 dopamine receptors (Soares-Cunha et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2004; Montague et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Slower baseline dopamine changes in tonic activity are believed to invigorate physical action based on cost-benefit tradeoffs.
source: Slower baseline dopamine changes in tonic activity are believed to invigorate physical action (Niv et al., 2007) based on cost-benefit tradeoffs (Salamone et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Striatal dopamine mediates the decision to apply cognitive control based on perceived value vs costs of doing so.
source: More recent work extended this framework and proposed that the same circuits subserve cost-benefit analysis of applying cognitive effort, framing the role of striatal dopamine as mediating the decision to apply cognitive control based on perceived value vs costs of doing so (Westbrook et al., 2021; Cools, 2016; Cools, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Both sulpiride and methylphenidate comparatively increased the willingness to exert cognitive effort, particularly in subjects with low striatal dopamine availability.
source: In a recent study that combined neurochemical imaging with pharmacological administration of 400 mg of sulpiride (another D2 dopamine receptor antagonist) and methylphenidate (a drug that boosts striatal dopamine availability) showed that both drugs comparatively increased the willingness to exert cognitive effort, particularly in subjects with low striatal dopamine availability (Westbrook et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Drugs that target D2 receptors mainly act on presynaptic D2 receptors at low doses, while binding to postsynaptic receptors prevailingly accounts for their effects at higher doses.
source: An important aspect of drugs that target D2 receptors is that they are known to mainly act on presynaptic D2 receptors at low doses, while binding to postsynaptic receptors prevailingly accounts for their effects at higher doses (Schoemaker et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior pharmacological research.

claim: Presynaptic D2 receptors are believed to play an autoregulatory control of dopamine signalling through inhibition of synthesis and dopamine release.
source: Presynaptic D2 receptors are believed to play an autoregulatory control of dopamine signalling through inhibition of synthesis and dopamine release (Ford, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The effects of amisulpride on model-based behaviour are not driven by postsynaptic effects but might rather be due to amisulpride increasing dopamine levels through presynaptic D2 receptor blockade and thereby boosting the willingness to apply cognitive effort.
source: Taken together, this provides some evidence for the notion that the effects of amisulpride on model-based behaviour are not driven by postsynaptic effects but might rather be due to amisulpride increasing dopamine levels through presynaptic D2 receptor blockade and thereby boosting the willingness to apply cognitive effort.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the serum level findings.

claim: Activation of D2 receptors was shown to lead to choice perseverance and more deterministic behaviour in animal studies.
source: In animal studies, activation of D2 receptors was shown to lead to choice perseverance and more deterministic behaviour
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to prior animal studies.

claim: D2 receptor inhibition increases the probability of performing competing actions and increases randomness in action selection in animal studies.
source: whereas D2 receptor inhibition increases the probability of performing competing actions and increases randomness in action selection (Sridharan et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior animal study.

claim: D2 receptor availability in the striatum correlated with choice uncertainty parameters across both reinforcement learning and active inference computational modelling frameworks in humans.
source: In humans, a recent neurochemical imaging study showed that D2 receptor availability in the striatum correlated with choice uncertainty parameters across both reinforcement learning and active inference computational modelling frameworks (Adams et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior human study.

claim: Increased choice uncertainty was observed in a social and non-social learning tasks in a study using 800 mg of sulpiride.
source: Increased choice uncertainty was also observed in a social and non-social learning tasks in a study using 800 mg of sulpiride, a dose that is known to exert post-synaptic effects (Eisenegger et al., 2014; Mikus et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: 50 mg of naltrexone leads to a~90% of µ receptor occupancy even 48 hr post intake.
source: The lack of a pronounced effect of naltrexone on model-based/model-free behaviour is unlikely to be due to issues of dosage or timing, since 50 mg of naltrexone leads to a~90% of µ receptor occupancy even 48 hr post intake (Lee et al., 1988; Trøstheim et al., 2022)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior pharmacological studies.

claim: Opioid receptor blockade leads to decreased sensitivity to reward value and accelerated habitual control of actions in rats.
source: In particular, a study in rats showed that opioid receptor blockade leads to decreased sensitivity to reward value and accelerated habitual control of actions (Wassum et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior animal study.

claim: µ opioid receptor availability correlated with goal-directed behaviour in a loss-only version of the two-step task in humans.
source: and in a recent neurochemical imaging study in humans µ opioid receptor availability correlated with goal-directed behaviour in a loss-only version of the two-step task (Voon et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior human study.

claim: Opioid agonists (but not antagonists) can in some cases lead to increased performance in cognitive control tasks.
source: In fact, opioid agonists (but not antagonists) can in some cases lead to increased performance in cognitive control tasks (van Steenbergen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior review.

claim: Naltrexone simply reduced the intrinsic value of reward and therefore decreased the motivation to exert cognitive effort.
source: One explanation of our results is that naltrexone simply reduced the intrinsic value of reward and therefore decreased the motivation to exert cognitive effort, which would be in line with the observed flattening of both positive and negative affect after naltrexone administration.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the naltrexone findings.

claim: Depletion of the serotonin precursor tryptophane biases behaviour towards habitual and away from goal-directed.
source: Most notably, depletion of the serotonin precursor tryptophane biases behaviour towards habitual and away from goal-directed (Worbe et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Serotonin terminal density in the striatum correlated with higher goal-directed behaviour in a version of the two-step task.
source: This claim is also in line with a recent neurochemical imaging study that showed that serotonin terminal density in the striatum correlated with higher goal-directed behaviour in a version of the two-step task (Voon et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Decreasing prefrontal serotonin levels has been shown to promote drug seeking behaviour.
source: and decreasing prefrontal serotonin levels has been shown to promote drug seeking behaviour (Pelloux et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Amisulpride also blocks serotonin receptors, albeit with lower affinity.
source: In light of this, we also note that amisulpride also blocks serotonin receptors, albeit with lower affinity
evidence: This is a statement about the pharmacological properties of amisulpride.

claim: D2 dopamine antagonists might promote goal-directed behaviour when alternative habitual choices are available, already in low doses.
source: Our results suggest that D2 dopamine antagonists might promote goal-directed behaviour when alternative habitual choices are available, already in low doses
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Opioid blockade does not have an effect on model-based behaviour.
source: while opioid blockade does not have such an effect on model-based behaviour
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The study took place in the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy at the Medical University of Vienna.
source: The study took place in the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy at the Medical University of Vienna.
evidence: This describes the location of the study.

claim: Participants underwent a physical examination (electrocardiogram, hemogram) and a psychiatric screening before being subjected to the two-step task.
source: After initial online screening, the participants were invited for a first visit, where they underwent a physical examination (electrocardiogram, hemogram) and a psychiatric screening before being subjected to the two-step task
evidence: This describes the study procedures.

claim: The two-step task consisted of a 25 min automated training period followed by 200 trials of the task.
source: that consisted of a 25 min automated training period followed by 200 trials of the task
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: After a waiting period of 3 hr, participants solved two additional tasks before performing the two-step task (on average 4 hr 36 min, SD = 22 min, after the pill intake).
source: After a waiting period of 3 hr, participants solved two additional tasks (explained elsewhere Korb et al., 2020) before performing the two-step task (on average 4 hr 36 min, SD = 22 min, after the pill intake)
evidence: This describes the timing of the study procedures.

claim: Waiting times and the doses of drugs were chosen based on previous pharmacological studies with the same compounds.
source: Waiting times and the doses of drugs were chosen based on previous pharmacological studies with the same compounds (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the study design, supported by citation.

claim: Blood plasma levels confirmed amisulpride levels above 212.6 µg/l (mean (sd)=548.8 (96.9)), in all participants of the amisulpride group.
source: Blood plasma levels confirmed amisulpride levels above 212.6 µg/l (mean (sd)=548.8 (96.9)), in all participants of the amisulpride group.
evidence: This describes the measured drug levels in participants.

claim: Data were collected from 120 volunteers and constituted a subset of volunteers involved in a larger study.
source: Data were collected from 120 volunteers and constituted a subset of volunteers involved in a larger study (Korb et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the sample and its relation to a larger study.

claim: For six participants the task data from the first session were lost due to failures in assigning screening codes from the first session to subject ID numbers in the second.
source: For six participants the task data from the first session were lost due to failures in assigning screening codes from the first session to subject ID numbers in the second.

source: For two participants the task data from the second session were lost owing to technical issues, resulting in 112 participants included in the main analysis
evidence: This describes data loss and final sample size.

claim: All participants had no history of drug abuse or other psychiatric disorders and were matched in age, sex, and BMI.
source: All participants had no history of drug abuse or other psychiatric disorders and were matched in age, sex, and BMI (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria and matching.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Medical University of Vienna (EK N. 1393/2017) and was in line with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Medical University of Vienna (EK N. 1393/2017) and was in line with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical association Declaration of Helsinki, 2013).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval of the study.

claim: Participants received a monetary compensation of 90€ plus the extra money earned in the task.
source: Participants received a monetary compensation of 90€ plus the extra money earned in the task.
evidence: This describes the participant compensation.

claim: In the task, participants made an initial choice at stage one which took them to one of the two possible states ('planets') in stage two.
source: In the task, participants made an initial choice at stage one which took them to one of the two possible states ('planets') in stage two.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: There were two possible states in the first stage, each featuring a pair of spaceships.
source: There were two possible states in the first stage, each featuring a pair of spaceships.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Each of the spaceships flew deterministically to one of the two planets where they encountered an alien who gave them either positive or negative points.
source: Each of the spaceships flew deterministically to one of the two planets where they encountered an alien who gave them either positive or negative points.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: The points in each planet changed according to a Gaussian random walk in the interval [–4, 5], rounded to whole numbers.
source: The points in each planet changed according to a Gaussian random walk in the interval [–4, 5], rounded to whole numbers.
evidence: This describes the reward structure of the task.

claim: Participants had 2000 ms to choose in the first step and then again 2000ms to press the space bar once they had encountered the alien.
source: Participants had 2000 ms to choose in the first step and then again 2000ms to press the space bar once they had encountered the alien.
evidence: This describes the timing constraints of the task.

claim: Each acquired point was translated to 4 Eurocents and added to the overall compensation of the participant at the end of the experiment.
source: Each acquired point was translated to 4 Eurocents and added to the overall compensation of the participant at the end of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the incentive structure of the task.

claim: The Gaussian random walks had various drift rates (0.5, 1, and 2).
source: To avoid all participants behaving in a model-based way (Feher da Silva and Hare, 2020) we increased the difficulty of the task by dynamically changing the drift of the reward-determining Gaussian walks. The Gaussian random walks, therefore, had various drift rates (0.5, 1, and 2).
evidence: This describes the task design to increase difficulty.

claim: Each participant first went through an automated rigorous explanation of the task followed by 25 practice trials before completing 200 trials of the task.
source: Each participant first went through an automated rigorous explanation of the task followed by 25 practice trials before completing 200 trials of the task.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the task.

claim: A hierarchical Bayesian approach was used in all analyses to regularize inference.
source: To regularize our inference, we used a hierarchical Bayesian approach in all our analyses.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used.

claim: Model M1 has better out of sample predictive accuracy compared to the other two models.
source: When comparing the performance of the three models we found that the model M1 has better out of sample predictive accuracy compared to the other two models (Fig. S1b).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: The mean (SD) posterior prediction accuracy of model M1 was 65% (11%).
source: To validate the novel model M1, we first used the posterior means of the estimated parameters to simulate behaviour in both sessions. To see how well we can retrieve the model parameters we reran the parameter estimation on the simulated behaviour with the same model (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and d). We also ran the same analysis of staying behaviour on this synthetic dataset and reproduced the behavioural plots from Figure 3 (compare to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and e). We used the same logistic hierarchical Bayesian model to statistically evaluate the crucial aspects of the behavioural analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and e, compare to Figure 3c). To get the posterior predictive accuracy of the model we predicted the choice on each trial for each participant for 8000 samples drawn from the posterior distribution and then calculated the average accuracy for each participant.
evidence: This is a finding from model validation analysis.
